title: Resolving difficult merge conflicts
description: Learn about Resolving difficult merge conflicts. Master the concepts, patterns, and best practices.

data.text: Merge conflicts happen when Git cannot automatically combine changes from two branches. Difficult conflicts involve large overlapping changes, renamed files, or binary files.

data.title: Lesson Scope
data.text: This lesson covers conflict markers, merge strategies, merge tools, diff3 format, file-level conflicts, and practical workflows for resolving complex conflicts.
What Is a Merge Conflict?

A conflict occurs when the same lines are changed in both branches being merged. Git pauses and marks the conflicted regions in the affected files. The developer must manually choose which changes to keep.

data.title: Conflict Output
data.code:
Auto-merging src/auth/login.ts
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in src/auth/login.ts
Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.

data.text: Conflict Markers
Git inserts conflict markers into files. Everything between <<<<<<< and ======= is the current branch version. Everything between ======= and >>>>>>> is the incoming branch version.

data.title: Conflict Markers
data.code:
<<<<<<< HEAD
const token = legacyParse(request);
=======
const token = modernParse(request);
>>>>>>> feature/new-parser

data.title: Understand the Markers
data.text: HEAD is your current branch. The other side is the branch being merged. Remove the markers and keep the correct code after resolving.
Resolving a Conflict
Open the conflicted file, remove the conflict markers, and keep the correct code. After resolving all conflicts, stage the files and complete the merge with git commit.

data.title: Resolving and Committing
data.code:
# Edit the conflicted file, remove markers, keep correct code

# Stage the resolved file
git add src/auth/login.ts

# Complete the merge
git commit -m "merge: resolve auth login conflict"

data.text: Aborting a Merge
If a merge becomes too complex, abort it to return to the pre-merge state. You can then reconsider the approach, pull in more context, or ask for help.

data.title: Aborting a Merge
data.code: git merge --abort

data.text: Merge Tools
Visual merge tools make resolving conflicts faster. Popular tools include VS Code's built-in merge editor, Meld, Beyond Compare, KDiff3, and P4Merge.

data.title: Configuring a Merge Tool
data.code:
git config --global merge.tool vscode

# Or for Meld
git config --global merge.tool meld

data.title: Launching a Merge Tool
data.code: git mergetool

data.text: Diff3 Format
Diff3 shows three versions of a conflicted section: yours, the common ancestor, and theirs. This extra context helps you understand what each side changed and why.

data.title: Enabling Diff3
data.code: git config --global merge.conflictstyle diff3

data.title: Diff3 Conflict Output
data.code:
<<<<<<< HEAD
const token = legacyParse(request);
||||||| common ancestor
const token = parse(request);
=======
const token = modernParse(request);
>>>>>>> feature/new-parser

data.title: Use Diff3 for Complex Conflicts
data.text: When you are unsure why a conflict occurred, enable diff3 to see the common ancestor. This often reveals the root cause quickly.
The ORT Merge Strategy

ORT is the modern default merge strategy in Git. It handles renames better than older strategies and produces cleaner merge results. For most daily merges, no action is needed; Git uses ORT automatically.

data.title: Specifying ORT
data.code: git merge -s ort feature/branch

data.text: The Recursive Merge Strategy
Recursive was the older default. It is still supported and can be useful when you need specific options such as patience or diff-algorithm tweaks. For new repositories, prefer ORT.

data.title: Recursive with Patience
data.code: git merge -s recursive -X patience feature/branch

data.text: File-Level Conflicts

Sometimes a conflict affects an entire file because it was deleted in one branch and modified in another. Git marks this as a delete/modify conflict and requires you to decide whether to keep or remove the file.

data.title: Delete/Modify Conflict
data.code: CONFLICT (delete/modify): src/old-module.ts deleted in HEAD and modified in feature/new-module. Version feature/new-module of src/old-module.ts left in tree.

data.title: Resolving Delete/Modify Conflict
data.code:
# Keep the modified version
git add src/old-module.ts

# Or remove it entirely
git rm src/old-module.ts

data.text: Rename Conflicts
Rename conflicts occur when both branches rename the same file to different names, or when one branch renames a file and the other modifies it. Git may not always detect these automatically.

items: Check git status to see all conflicted files
Use git log --follow to trace file history through renames
Manually decide which renamed version to keep
Stage the resolution with git add

data.title: Rename Detection Is Imperfect
data.text: Git rename detection is heuristic-based. If a conflict seems wrong, inspect the file history manually with git log --follow before resolving.
Submodule Conflicts
Submodule conflicts happen when different branches point to different commits of the same submodule. Resolve by choosing the correct submodule commit and updating the superproject.

data.title: Resolving Submodule Conflicts
data.code:
# Check which submodules are conflicted
git status

# Set the submodule to the correct commit
git add path/to/submodule

# Complete the merge
git commit

data.text: Large File Conflicts

Merging large binary files such as images, PDFs, or archives is problematic because Git cannot auto-merge them. One side wins entirely. If both sides modified the binary, you must manually choose or combine them.

items: Use git lfs for large binary files
Avoid committing generated binaries to Git
If a binary conflict occurs, decide which version to keep
Consider storing large files in artifact storage instead

data.text: Merge Conflict Workflow

items: Run git status to list all conflicted files
Open each conflicted file and resolve markers
Use git mergetool for visual assistance if needed
Run git add on resolved files
Run git commit to finalize the merge
Run the test suite to verify the result

data.title: Full Conflict Resolution Workflow
data.code:
git merge feature/complex-change

# See conflicts
git status

# Resolve in editor or with mergetool
# ... editing ...

# Stage resolved files
git add src/auth/login.ts src/api/users.ts

# Commit the resolution
git commit

data.text: Preventing Conflicts

items: Keep branches short-lived and merge frequently
Coordinate with teammates before touching shared files
Use feature flags instead of long-lived branches
Agree on code formatting to reduce whitespace conflicts
Configure .gitattributes for merge drivers on generated files

data.title: Gitattributes for Generated Files
data.code:
# Never auto-merge generated files - use theirs
generated/*.js merge=ours

# Use a custom merge driver for lockfiles
package-lock.json merge=package-lock

data.text: Communication During Conflicts

When a conflict involves another team member's work, communicate before resolving. Ask what their intent was, especially if the conflict is in a complex area like database migrations or API contracts.

items: Tag the other author in a comment on the PR or issue
Explain why the conflict occurred and what you chose
Share the resolved code for a quick sanity check
Document non-obvious resolutions in a team wiki

data.title: Conflict Resolution Is a Team Activity
data.text: Do not resolve difficult conflicts silently. A brief note explaining the choice prevents future confusion and helps teammates learn.
Summary
Difficult merge conflicts are inevitable in collaborative development. Understanding conflict markers, merge strategies, and visual merge tools makes resolution faster and safer.

data.title: Key Takeaways
text: Use conflict markers to understand what each side changed
Use diff3 for extra context on complex conflicts
Use visual merge tools to speed resolution
Prevent conflicts with short-lived branches and communication
